here's the long answer:  the national fire protection association (nfpa) says replace every 10 years, regardless of whether it tests ok or not.  specifically, nfpa 72 (the national fire alarm code) states, "unless otherwise recommended by the manufacturer's published instructions, single- and multiple-stations smoke alarms installed in one- and two-family dwellings shall be replaced when they fail to respond to operability tests, but shall not remain in service longer than 10 years from the date of manufacture."  note "...from date of manufacture.", which could be many months prior to date of purchase or installation.  for example, an alarm manufactured in april 2014 and bought in july 2015, should be replaced in april 2024 or sooner if it fails to respond to operability tests (i.e., the 'push to test' button).  better safe than sorry, imho.  the date of manufacture is indicated on the label on the back of each smoke alarm.  hope this helps.

i was also worried about damaging my violin when i was looking through possible pickups to buy -that is the beauty if this pickup design; its doesn't involve invasive installation, and can be removed at any time.   attached to the mike (the disk shape with the cherub logo imprint) is the spring-loaded, crescent-shaped arm that you pull back and slip inside the f hole of your instrument.  the arm holds the mike in close contact with your instrument, but doesn't damage it in any way. the fact that i didn't have to alter my instrument at all was the deciding factor in my purchasing the cherub pickup.  its quick and easy to use!  i'm not sure how the sound quality compares with other, more expensive pickups -but the rest of my band can certainly hear me now.
very carefully.  it did scratch my violin when i first put it on.

the flat surface of the pickup that makes contact with the top of your viola is a soft thin rubber disc, the size of a quarter, the other piece of the spring loaded clip is soft and rubber and it goes inside. it won't even scratch the inside. there is no way i can imagine it doing any damage as long as you don't trip over the wire. this is a cheap little device that for the money, does a pretty good job. get a 1/4" female to male extension cable if you need more distance from your amplified and speaker to avoid feedback. to honest, this little thing works quite a bit better than i expected. when you get good paying job on stage buy an expensive one or an electric viola. it beats using a microphone and costs much less.

the unit is a clip setup where the top of the clip is the contact for sound and the bottom is just a u-shaped bar that pinches it against the wood from inside. as long the f-holes on your instrument aren't too small it should fit in without touching anything else and no real risk for damage. only real danger is that you might knock over the sound post when you're sliding it around for a good spot.

it's quite easy. the bottom's curve stick is what opens up as a clip, that's what you insert in the f hole. then you turn it sideways counterclockwise, release the clip mechanism gently and you are set. good luck!
the spring clip fits nicely through the f hole and holds the pickup firmly against the top of your viola.

as other people said, the small arm rests on the inside of the violin through the f-hole. something you should be careful of is the spring loaded clip has no opposing lip on the mic side to get a solid grasp when removing it. this means it's easy to lose your grip when removing the mic causing it to slap back down on your violin and sometimes flinging the clip arm or the mic into the delicate parts of your f-hole. the best way to solve this would be for the manufacturer to put a lip on the top of the mic that would allow you to grip the mic better allowing for safer removal. that said, it is a great mic and causes no damage when used properly and as long as you're careful inserting and removing it.

hi hakeem -this switch does not have anything other than dedicated ethernet ports.  they are all the same.for clarity, most modern networking hardware supports a feature known as auto-mdi-x.  what that feature does is it eliminates the need for crossover cables.  crossover cables simply 'cross over' one or two pairs of wires (depending on the ieee spec you're working with).  this is done so that transmit on one end always ends up at receiver on the other end when connecting like devices.do not mistake this device for a router that does have a dedicated wan (uplink) port.  if you plug your cable modem into this switch you will probably be limited to connecting one device only.hope that helps.jimjim

carbon steel is easy to keep sharp but it will rust very easily. even wiping a blade with a paper towel leaves a little moisture behind. coating the blade with just a tiny amount of food grade mineral oil can help prevent rust.

hey bryce, the mora knife you have is a high carbon steel blade with a satin finish. this blade is great for survivalist because high carbon blades can be struck against flint or churt or even quarts on the  back of the blade to create sparks for starting a fire. the down side to high carbon steel is it will eventually loose the satin finish and get a patina like old guns do. you have to handle this blade with a little care. use gun oil or even furniture polish to keep the blade from rusting and keep it looking good. no matter what it will eventually get a patina but that is different from rust. rust is bad and can be removed with a light steel wool. mora does make stainless steel blades that resist rust and patina very well but stainless steel is much harder to sharpen and they cant be used to create sparks to make fire. i hope this helps.
it's a high carbon blade. clean it with steel wool and keep lightly covered with cooking oil.

if you leave moisture on it the outside can turn a brownish color, its nothing to worry about and will rub off with a bit of elbow grease and a microfiber cloth, some people like to oil them a bit after washing, but the key is making sure its nice and dry before storing it again. there are products like break-free clp or even wd-40 would work, you just want something to displace the moisture, a quick towel drying will likely leave a moisture film, i always dry with microfiber to avoid this. if you ever see the blade turning a more reddish color, that's rust and means you aren't keep it clean and dry.

the blade is made of carbon steel - not stainless steel. carbon steel is generally easier to sharpen and holds a better edge. the down side is that it requires one more step to finish after usage. you will need to wipe a thin application of either mineral oil or vegetable oil on it to prevent rusting. for me the trade off is worth it as i prefer carbon steel. you can renew that blade to near original look by polishing it with a very fine grade of sandpaper or emery cloth. even a scotch brite pad will go a long way to brighten the blade. you still finish with mineral oil. good luck, they are fine blade of the "old school" of manufacture at a reasonable price.

mora is a high carbon steel so it will stain over time. does not take away from the quality of the blade. mora's aren't meant to be pretty, they are meant to be used. if the rust freaks you out, just use a mild abrasive to remove it then use a light coat of oil on the blade. any oil will do. i use olive oil since it is food friendly. it will last you a lifetime.

carbon steel oxidizes much easier than "stainless" (there is no true stainless, just some more resistant than others). carbon steel has many other great properties i won't get into here, but as has been said, a little oil (food grade like mineral oil is more appropriate of you will cut food, or it is a possibility) will help prevent overt rust. a forced patina (making the blade oxidize in a more limited and controlled way) is a way to actually further prevent rust. exposure to various light acids for limited times helps, such as cutting citrus or soaking with vinegar.

here's the short (but somewhat deceptive) answer: 1 candlepower = 12.57 lumens. but in order to interpret that statement, you need to understand that candlepower and lumens do not actually measure the same thing.candlepower is most useful as a measure of illumination in a particular direction, while lumens are most useful as a measure of total illumination. the conversion above is saying that a light source shining with 1 candlepower in all directions would produce 12.57 lumens.imagine you're in a dark room with just a thin beam of sunlight shining through a tiny opening between heavy curtains. that beam represents high candlepower, but modest lumens. you wouldn't want to look straight into the direction it's coming from, even though the sunbeam doesn't brighten the whole room much. on the other hand, a table lamp could brighten the room much more than that sunbeam, even though it's not nearly as bright as the sun when you look directly at it. that lamp represents high lumens, but modest candlepower. see the difference?if you'd like to know more, have a look at this article, "measuring light intensity":http://www.energybooks.com/pdf/d1150.pdfoh, and if you're mathematically inclined, the origin of the factor 12.57 is simple--it's actually just 4*pi. that's also the basis for the number 8% in the "candlepower" section of the article i cited, because 1/12.57 = 8%.reply with quote

the light's description says it uses a 130w h4 halogen lamp. a halogen lamps emits between 16 and 24 lumens per watt, putting the range of feasible answers begins as a number between 2,080 and 3,120. assuming it not made with the overpriced short lived 24 lumen/watt halogen, and allowing for some lost light not captured by the reflector or dissipated in the front lens ... the light puts out something between 1800 and 2000 lumens.a previously supplied answer is correct insofar as the usefulness of candlepower goes, but erroneously states a conversion factor. the conversion from lumens to cp depends on the angular width of the projected light beam. finally, because sales go to the light claiming the most candlepower, spotlights advertise the peak hot spot in the beam, not an average intensity of the beam. 12,000,000 cp will be several times the average beam intensity.

i have an 1800.  i use a 12/3, for my 100' driveway.  i live in the northeast.  i am very happy with this blower because it will throw the slushy and wet snow without clogging, my 2 stage gas powered 10 horse machine will always clog.  in fact i find no need for the big gas powered thing, haven't touched it for about 4 years.  i cannot tell the difference between the cords when i have used a 12/3 or 14/3 or 16/3.  this is why i use a 12/3....think of the electric cord as a "garden hose", and you are trying to force 120 gallons per minute through the hose.   which will be easier forcing 120 gallons through a 1/2"  hose or through a 1" hose.  the 1" because there is less resistance to flow because the inside of the hose is wider.  so if the toro 1800 is trying to draw 120 volts (household current), which will be easier?... through a 16/3 guage (small narrow cord) or the thicker 12/3 (wider cord).   so that means your toro 1800 won't be working as hard with the larger cord 12/3, and it will let the motor last longer.  the draw backs are that the 12/3 is heavy at 100' feet in length.  also more "work" for the blower to draw current through 100' than it is across 50 feet.  so i installed a lamp post with an outlet half way up my 100' driveway.  still trying to be nice to the electric motor so that it will last longer.  now with the lamp post, i use about a 60-70 foot  "12/3 cord".  my only other advice is try to make sure there are no rocks on your driveway.  they have a habit of jamming in the auger, stopping the augers movement, while the electric motor is still trying to turn the paddle/auger.  i did burn out a toro 1800 motor this way.

nathan got it right.  you may not notice any difference between 12 and 16 gauge extension cords, but the motor's lifespan will be shortened.  the more amps an electric motor is rated and/or the length of the cord determine the desired gauge of the extension cord.  there are formulas available to determine recommended gauge.if you need 100 feet of extension cord, do yourself a favor and buy two 50 foot cords.  you will pay a little more in comparison to one 100 foot cord, but it is much easier to untangle (and it will get tangled) and to coil up for storage.  i use the wrap-around-the-shoulder method to coil my extension cords and i run out of shoulder at about 65 feet.  plus you can use just one cord to start with, which helps keep the cord from being hard to manage.  once you have extended one cord, add the other.

no it does not and my experience is that you won't need a different stylus if you have the stylus height adjusted correctly.  you should be able to judge the center/point of the stylus as it passes over the original if you have the various adjustments correct.  the bit size is paramount.  on fine work start with the a small diameter bit to do the fine work.  then go to a wider bit for larger areas.  caution when changing out bits!... be sure to keep the depth of the cut identical for both bits.  and, it is a good idea to test your cut with a piece of scrap but scrap of the same type of material.  stylus diameter shouldn't matter.  if you have trouble seeing where the center of the stylus is you might try putting a dab of paint on the end of the stylus by doint this: take a piece of paper with a drop of dark paint on it under the stylus and then carefully dip the stylus in the paint to a depth of say 1/32 of an inch.  that should make the very bottom of the stylus more clearly visible.  be sure to allow the paint to completely dry before using... and remember the stylus usually doesn't need to touch the original.  the only exception is when doing 3d carvings.  when doing 3d the paint can first be removed with a little paint thinner. this removes any chance of the paint marking the original
